newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany still hunting Nazi war crimes suspects.
newsitem.headline: Germany still hunting Nazi war crimes suspects.

text.p: BONN, May 24 - German prosecutors are still investigating hundreds of suspected Nazi war criminals, most of whom are now in their 80s and 90s, the news magazine Spiegel reported on Saturday.

Prosecutor Willi Dressen, the new head of Germany's Nazi war crimes investigations office, told Spiegel in an interview released ahead of publication on Monday about 25 preliminary cases were still pending which listed hundreds of suspects.

He said files from the East Berlin's Ministry for State Security (Stasi) archives were being evaluated and that prosecutors had already identified 37 new suspects and were assessing 50 other potential cases.
Many of Adolf Hitler's top henchmen were tried and executed by the Allied powers after the Nuremberg trials that opened in 1946, charged with crimes against humanity and war crimes.
But in the chaotic aftermath of World War Two, thousands of less well known perpetrators changed their names and identities to lead new lives.
Of about 80,000 German war crimes suspects, only about 1,300 decided against changing their identity, fearing they would implicate themselves in additional crimes, Dressen said.

"The number of those still living under false names is not higher than 1,000," he said, adding he was disappointed with the office's success since 1945 -- only 6,500 Nazi war crimes convictions out of 106,000 accused.

"At the moment we have 25 preliminary cases against several hundred people. We are working through documents from the former East German Stasi. In 37 cases we have already handed over documents to prosecutors," Dressen said.

He said the office's greatest disaster was in failing to catch Mauthausen concentration camp doctor, Aribert Heim, who prosecutors believe killed hundreds of inmates by using them as human guinea pigs in gruesome medical experiments.
"That he was never caught and that after the war he lived a good life, that's really bitter," Dressen said of the man, who is still wanted by prosecutors.
